data.title: FedEx targets cross-border ecommerce challenges with Global Trade Navigator tools
data.description:
FedEx launched a new set of digital trade tools it designed to help businesses in a dynamic global environment to navigate tariffs, customs requirements and cross-border shipping costs before packages reach international borders.

The carrier designed its new tools, packaged under the name Global Trade Navigator, to enable businesses to look up tariff codes, estimate duties and taxes, and identify potential customs issues earlier in the shipping process, according to FedEx.

The tools, announced Sept. 9, span the full international shipping workflow from pre-shipment planning through customs clearance reporting. They are available to businesses at a range of sizes from small to enterprise scale.

More than 900 of North America’s Top 2000 largest online retailers use FedEx as a shipping carrier, according to Digital Commerce 360 data. Retailers that used FedEx for fulfillment reported a combined $789.51 billion in 2025 ecommerce sales.

How FedEx’s Global Trade Navigator tools work

The suite covers five areas of the international shipping process:

  1. Pre-shipping planning. Free, self-service guidance on estimated duties, taxes, fees, and document recommendations. Businesses do not need a login for this information.
  2. Shipment data. Customers can review product code classifications, customs values, and country of manufacture information.
  3. Checkout cost transparency. Sellers can display duty and tax information to customers through Shopify, providing more transparency into import costs.
  4. Integrate trade insights. Allows businesses to incorporate product classifications, estimated duties and taxes, and regulatory information into existing systems.
  5. Clearance and reporting management. FedEx customers can use these tools to view customs clearances. They can also find out what actions they’re required to take, manage payments and more. 

Impact of duties on ecommerce

Retailers have faced complications stemming from changing tariffs — and later refunds — in the U.S. throughout 2025 and 2026. 68% of small and medium-sized businesses report that customers are regularly surprised by duties at delivery, according to FedEx’s 2026 Small Business Trade Index, which surveyed 1,000 small-business decision makers.

“International shipping requires businesses to make complex decisions long before a package begins its journey,” said Jason Brenner, senior vice president of digital portfolio at FedEx, in a written statement. “Building on decades of global trade expertise, Global Trade Navigator makes critical trade information and guidance more accessible to businesses as they grow internationally.”

Ultimately, Brenner pitched Global Trade Navigator as a solution to achieve what he said would be “fewer surprises and a more predictable experience for businesses and consumers.”

FedEx Q4 results

In its fiscal Q4 ended May 31, FedEx reported $25.0 billion in revenue, an increase of 12.6% year over year. For the full fiscal year, the shipping provider’s income grew 7.7% to $94.7 billion. 

International export packages from the U.S. grew 5% year over year in Q4, marking the second straight quarter of growth. 

Prior to the announcement of the new Global Trade Navigator tools, FedEx executives referred to complications customers faced with international trade in an earnings call.

“We have continued to help our customers navigate a very dynamic and complex environment: the implementation of global trade policy changes, geopolitical unrest in the Middle East, and the IEEPA refund process,” said Brie Carere, chief customer officer at FedEx.

data.title: Rugs Direct adds AI assistant Ask Cleo for site search, PDP support
data.description:
Rugs Direct has rolled out its on-site AI-powered conversational assistant, Ask Cleo, and it’s driving increases in key performance indicators.

The retailer falls under Elevated Brands Group, also the parent company Lightopia. Elevated Brands Group launched Ask Cleo as separate rollouts for each retailer. Lightopia debuted Ask Cleo on its site in May, with Rugs Direct following weeks later, in early June.

Sharon Gautschi, chief merchandising officer of Elevated Brands Group, shared that since then, add-to-cart rates for consumers using Ask Cleo have been 8x to 9x more than other users across both Rugs Direct and Lightopia.

“But you do have to temper that with engagement,” Gautschi told Digital Commerce 360. “Certainly, the majority of customers are still using classic search. So that is a higher add-to-cart rate, but on a smaller base. We’re still ramping up engagement.”

Using agentic AI to power its search, Ask Cleo allows shoppers to describe what they are looking for conversationally. It can ask clarifying questions and help solve practical design challenges such as selecting an appropriate fixture for a vaulted ceiling, according to Elevated Brands Group.

Rugs Direct is No. 622 in the Top 1000 Database. The market research tool tracks North America’s largest online retailers, ranking them by annual ecommerce sales and more.

Rugs Direct is also No. 492 in Digital Commerce 360’s new AI Rankings. That set of rankings is available in the Top 1000 Pro with AI Database.

How Rugs Direct and Lightopia are using AI agents for search

Consumer shopping both Rugs Direct and Lightopia are “really showing us that they are looking for quality,” Gautschi said. But there’s another set of customers chasing fashion, she added.

“They are clearly interested in using conversational or natural language search,” Gautschi explained. “And that’s becoming more and more prevalent across our industry, which is exciting and fun. They really want more answers, they want it fast and they want to understand the results.”

She shared that Elevated Brands Group tapped Constructor to develop Ask Cleo. Lightopia and Rugs Direct both use Ask Cleo in two different ways:

  • AI Shopping Assistant (ASA). Gautschi described this as a site-level or higher-funnel search tool.
  • Product Insights Agent (PIA). She described this tool as living on a product’s page to answer specific questions about it.

“Overall, we’ve seen some interesting trends where the more questions they ask, then the higher the KPIs are,” Gautschi said. “The signals are stronger. We’re seeing higher add-to-cart, higher purchase rates.”

Consumers on Rugs Direct might use Ask Cleo to learn about a rug’s materials, thickness and dimensions, she noted. On Lightopia’s site, they might use Ask Cleo more spec-focused questions, she said, as lighting is “much more technical” than rugs. That could mean asking about dimmability, ceiling height, bulb compatibility or color temperature.

How Elevated Brands Group trained its AI agent

Gautschi said Elevated Brands Group plays “a big part” in feeding information to train its AI agent. Elevated Brands Group has articles and blog posts that it has written for public relations and search engine optimization (SEO). It also has specifications for all its products.

Elevated Brands Group has taken that library of content and given it to Ask Cleo, according to Gautschi. The training process took about four to six weeks, she estimated. Ultimately, though, it comes down to bandwidth.

She also praised the company’s emphasis on data integrity.

“Even some of the larger companies I’ve worked with, getting one spec updated across my assortment is really hard, but here, we’re pretty nimble with data integrity,” Gautschi said. “And that’s able to feed the agents quite well, where the agents can really respond nicely.”

Using all that data, Rugs Direct and Lightopia have trained Ask Cleo on brand voice and how they want it to respond to consumers. Gautschi said the company intends for the Ask Cleo tool to function like a “well-informed friend with great design, style and taste.”

“It doesn’t just say, here’s what you want,” according to Gautschi. “It really should give you some advice and some additional things to think about for what you’re looking for. We feed it and then we test it, so we’ll ask it questions to see how it responds. And if it doesn’t respond in a way that we think is right — or the answer can be optimized — then we are giving those examples back to our third party.”

Off-site AI traffic to Lightopia, Rugs Direct

Gautschi noted that Rugs Direct and Lightopia are increasingly generating traffic from AI platforms such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, or Perplexity. She estimated that AI traffic referrals generate less than 10% of consumers’ visits to the two retailers’ sites.

“We are definitely getting more traffic from AI platforms, but not enough,” Gautschi said. “I want more. And as a smaller company — we’re not Wayfair, we’re not Walmart — we’re competing with those big guys. We’re definitely seeing the traffic come our way, and we have nowhere to go but up, fortunately, in terms of increasing that traffic.”

That growth in traffic could also help bring visibility to the online retailers’ Ask Cleo tool. If agentic AI-powered search platforms’ traffic becomes “more qualified,” she said, then Elevated Brands Group will expect return on investment (ROI) and return on ad spend (ROAS) to be higher than traditional digital paid marketing programs.

data.title: Instacart launches AI assistant Clementine, agentic commerce integrations
data.description:
Instacart has launched an artificial intelligence assistant, Clementine, for grocery shopping support while adding new partners for its existing enterprise AI tool Cart Assistant.

As of Sept. 9, Instacart users in North America can tap Clementine for “the hardest parts of grocery shopping,” according to the company. It referred to decisions such as what to make for a meal, “shopping the way a family actually eats” and staying within budget. Instacart said the AI assistant helps users develop a personalized cart in seconds. It added that it based the Clementine experience on “what’s actually available on shelves in real time from the customer’s chosen store, so people can spend less time figuring out what’s for dinner and more time actually enjoying it.”

Chris Rogers, CEO at Instacart, said in a statement that millions of families ask themselves what’s for dinner on a given night. They don’t know the answer or what to shop for, he added.

“We’ve spent nearly 15 years learning how families shop and eat, and Clementine puts that knowledge to work,” Rogers said. “It learns from the preferences you share and the way you’ve shopped on Instacart. It can help you stay on budget and surface what’s actually in stock at your chosen store, handling enough of the weekly planning that the mental load actually feels lighter.”

Instacart said early results show that its customers start with tasks such as restocking before using the AI tool for “higher-order use cases,” such as recipe discovery.

On average, Instacart said, customers placing orders through the Clementine AI assistant include more items than other users. Those customers using Clementine tend to also exceed $115 in average order value, according to Instacart.

How the Instacart Clementine AI assistant works

Instacart said its Clementine AI assistant factors in data from more than 1.6 billion lifetime orders and a catalog of more than 2 billion items. Additionally, Instacart said, Clementine uses more than 10 million daily inventory signals from about 100,000 locations across 2,200 retail operators in North America.

According to Instacart, that foundation powers its inventory intelligence, allowing the Clementine AI to understand what products are available in real time as well as what’s on sale at any given moment.

Instacart said its Clementine AI assistant can:

  • generate personalized recipes and display curated existing options
  • make suggestions based on a household’s dietary restrictions and preferences
  • help customers find deals and promotions, as well as lower-cost alternatives
  • reorder automatically
  • create occasion-centered shopping lists
  • upload grocery lists, whether handwritten or digital screenshots, converting them into lists of products to add to cart

“Grocery shopping is one of the most routine things people do, and also one of the most personal,” said John Adams, vice president and head of product at Instacart, in a statement. “What we built with Clementine is a system that understands both of those things — not just what you need, but how you eat, what you love, and what’s on the shelves at your store right now. Whatever you’re craving or planning for, Clementine can get you there. The more you use it, the more it feels like a natural part of how your household shops, becoming something you reach for week after week.”

Instacart adds partners for white-label AI tool Cart Assistant

In addition to Clementine, Instacart offers what it describes as a white-label AI tool, Cart Assistant. It said that tool is “for grocers who want to offer their own branded agentic shopping experience on their website and app.”

Instacart said the Cart Assistant combines its grocery data with a retailer’s catalog and customer data. That helps it to create a branded assistant that can suggest relevant deals and recipes. At the same time, it helps users to build carts without searching for products item by item. The company said grocers can customize the name, tone, loyalty integration and recipe content.

Instacart said current retailers using Cart Assistant include Food Bazaar, Heritage Grocers Group and Woodman’s. It said Harmon’s, The Save Mart, Stew Leonard’s and more companies will follow.

Additionally, Instacart said it has partnered with Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. It said grocery conversations that begin on Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini or AI Mode in Google Search “can be seamlessly completed on Instacart, where users can place an order from their preferred retailer for delivery or pickup.”

data.title: Circle-Tazapay deal aims to accelerate USDC adoption in cross-border B2B payments
data.description:
Circle Internet Group has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Tazapay, a Singapore-based business-to-business (B2B) cross-border payments company, in a deal aimed at accelerating adoption of its USDC stablecoin for global commerce.

Meanwhile, Tazapay brings more than $25 billion in annualized payment volume, banking in over 100 markets, and 60-plus fintech partners. Circle said that infrastructure will help make USDC a faster, more accessible payment rail across Asia-Pacific and emerging markets.

About Circle’s acquisition of Tazapay

The companies expect to close the acquisition in 2027 pending regulatory approvals, including sign-off from the Monetary Authority of Singapore. It deepens a relationship that began in 2025, when Tazapay served as a design partner for Circle Payments Network.

Approximately 60% of Tazapay’s existing transaction volume already involves stablecoins, according to Circle. That underscores how far the Singapore-based platform had already moved toward digital-asset settlement before announcing the deal. Circle is the issuer of USDC, one of the world’s largest dollar-backed stablecoins.

“Stablecoin settlement is becoming core infrastructure in the global economy, and combining USDC with Tazapay’s world-class banking relationships, local payout rails, and institutional customer base will accelerate worldwide USDC adoption,” said Jeremy Allaire, co-founder, CEO and chairman at Circle, in a press release. “Tazapay has been a design partner for Circle Payments Network since 2025 and we share a deep alignment. We are excited to bring the team in-house and work together towards accelerating Circle’s mission.”

Tazapay officials also heralded the move.

“We built Tazapay to make payments faster, remove friction, and streamline dependency on banking rails that don’t operate at the speed of global commerce,” said Rahul Shinghal, co-founder and CEO of Tazapay. “Circle has the dollar infrastructure in USDC and the regulatory standing to take what we’ve built further than we could alone. That’s what makes this the right move and what we’re focused on delivering together.”

Implications of increased USDC stablecoin adoption

Robin Anderson, head of product at Tribe Payments, said the deal shows where stablecoins are gaining traction.

“I don’t think we’re quite there yet on the consumer side — where people wake up and decide they want to pay with USDC,” Anderson said. “But on the payment infrastructure side, it’s a different conversation.”

Anderson noted that Tazapay already has payment rails across more than 100 markets.

“That gives Circle something it would take years to build from scratch — connections into local payment methods, currencies and regulatory environments, as well as an established base of businesses already moving money internationally. It creates a much more direct route for USDC to be used in real-world cross-border commerce,” Anderson said.

He noted stablecoins can help in cross-border payments to solve aspects such as:

  • settlement times
  • restricted banking hours
  • trapped liquidity
  • the number of intermediaries involved in the payment ecosystem

“This fits that use case well,” Anderson said. “However, stablecoins aren’t likely to replace the existing payment system wholesale. Businesses will still need reliable ways to move between stablecoins and local currencies, manage compliance and reach recipients who want to be paid through familiar local methods. Tazapay helps Circle bridge those two worlds.”

He observed that the customer at either end probably won’t know a stablecoin is involved.

“And I’m not sure they need to,” Anderson said. “If the money gets where it needs to go more quickly, predictably, and with fewer steps in between, that’s the part that counts. For me, this deal is another sign that stablecoins are starting to become part of the payment infrastructure rather than something sitting off to the side of it.”

data.title: Target deepens AI push, adding photo search and review insights
data.description:
Target is weaving artificial intelligence (AI) into more everyday shopping tasks, from finding products in a photo to picking up where shoppers left off online.

In a Sept. 8 blog post, the retailer highlighted several AI-powered shopping features it has rolled out since 2025. These include Photo Search, which lets shoppers upload images to find similar products, along with tools that summarize customer reviews, surface past purchases for reordering and bring shoppers back to items they recently viewed.

The update comes as Target puts more leadership behind its AI strategy. The retailer recently appointed Chandhu Nair as its first chief AI officer, effective Aug. 24. During Target’s quarterly earnings call last month, CEO Michael Fiddelke said Nair would help the company “accelerate how we harness the power of AI to create better guest experiences and unlock new capabilities across our business.”

Target is No. 5 in the Top 1000 Database. The market research tool tracks North America’s largest online retailers, ranking them by annual ecommerce sales and more.

Target is also No. 54 in Digital Commerce 360’s all-new AI Rankings. That set of rankings is available in the Top 1000 Pro with AI Database.

Target adds photo search and AI review summaries

Photo Search, the newest of Target’s AI tools, launched in August in the Target app.

Shoppers can tap the camera icon in the search bar, then upload or snap a photo to find similar products “without needing to describe them in words,” the company said.

Meanwhile, AI Review Insights tackles a different shopping task: sorting through dozens or even hundreds of customer reviews online.

Launched in June, the AI tool identifies a product’s commonly discussed attributes and organizes customer feedback into themes, helping shoppers focus on “the information that matters most to their purchase decision,” Target said. For example, the tool could group activewear reviews around topics such as comfort, fit, stretch and breathability.

Target said early results show Review Insights is boosting conversion and add-to-cart activity while reducing what it calls “decision fatigue,” though it did not share specific figures.

Neither of the features is unique to Target. Amazon, for example, has offered photo-based product search through Amazon Lens and AI-generated summaries of customer reviews for several years.

Target leverages AI for repeat purchases

Target is also using AI to simplify repeat purchases. Available through the app’s main navigation, its Buy Again tool surfaces a user’s past purchases, frequently ordered items and relevant deals based on previous shopping behavior. A shopper could pull up a recent grocery order, for example, and quickly add staples such as milk, bread or paper products to a new cart.

After launching Buy Again last year, Target said it has improved the tool’s recommendations and deal selection. The retailer said the experience has delivered “double-digit conversion growth year-over-year, while driving demand in categories like food and beverage.”

Meanwhile, Continue Shopping takes a similar approach to unfinished purchases. Using AI-powered personalization, the feature brings shoppers back to products they recently viewed while also surfacing alternatives and offers across Target’s homepage, My Target and search results. Since launching last fall, Target told Digital Commerce 360 that it is “driving double-digit conversion rates and incremental add-to-carts.”

Target expands AI shopping push

The tools are part of Target’s broader push into AI-driven commerce. On the company’s Q2 earnings call on Aug. 19, chief merchandising officer Cara Sylvester said Target had added AI-powered teacher and college wish lists, along with more personalized content on the app’s home screen.

She said total wish-list creations were up more than 50% from a year earlier, while the number of items added to those lists more than doubled. Conversion across Target’s key back-to-school pages also increased nearly 20%, she said.

Beyond its own app and website, Target is also looking at how shoppers can reach the retailer through outside AI platforms. Fiddelke said Target has partnered with OpenAI, Google Gemini and others as it explores agentic commerce.

Traffic to Target from external AI platforms remains small overall, he said, though its growth rate is more than 3.5 times that of the industry compared with a year ago.

Shipt launches Ask Shipt assistant

Target-owned Shipt is also rolling out its own AI shopping tool, adding another layer to the retailer’s push into conversational commerce. On Sept. 9, the same-day delivery service introduced Ask Shipt in its app and on Shipt.com.

Shipt, which Target acquired in 2017, describes Ask Shipt as an AI assistant that can turn prompts, recipes and meal photos into a shopping cart. Shoppers can describe what they need, and the assistant identifies relevant products and builds a cart. Users can then review, swap or edit its suggestions before checkout.

“Ask Shipt brings people-centric AI directly into the shopping journey, helping members move from inspiration to a personalized cart in moments,” said Katie Stratton, Shipt’s chief growth and strategy officer, in a statement.

Stratton said the tool works across Shipt’s marketplace of more than 100 retailer partners.

The launch comes as Shipt experiments with other conversational entry points. The company said it recently enabled shopping through ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude.

Shipt is also preparing to launch Shared Lists, which will let multiple users contribute to the same shopping list in real time. The feature can then convert the list into a cart with a single click.
